item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q004_ferritin_like_functional_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins, and manganese catalases within the ferritin-like fold (a.25) and ferritin-like superfamily (a.25.1), but in distinct families: ferritin (a.25.1.1), ribonucleotide-reductase-like (a.25.1.2), and manganese catalase (a.25.1.3). Thus, their shared helical core and metal-binding-site topology support remote homology/common ancestry, whereas their family separation reflects substantial functional divergence. Ferritins primarily store iron and perform ferroxidase chemistry; ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins include metal-dependent radical-generating or oxygen-activating components; manganese catalases disproportionate hydrogen peroxide using manganese. Superfamily membership alone does not justify transferring substrate, metal specificity, catalytic mechanism, active-site details, oligomeric state, or biological function. A cross-family structure may serve as a remote template for the conserved core, but family-matched representatives are required for functional inference and active-site modeling. Assignment of a particular chemistry needs external biochemical evidence such as metal analysis and catalytic assays, supported by sequence/structural examination of coordinating residues and, where relevant, genomic context.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
